title: How Teachers Can Use Large Language Models and Bloom’s Taxonomy to Create Educational Quizzes
venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models can help teachers create educational reading quizzes that are as good as or better than quizzes written entirely by hand. The authors focus on educational question generation (QG), arguing that although LLMs have shown strong technical performance, there has been limited evaluation of how teachers actually use generated questions in realistic practice. The study specifically asks whether teachers find automatically generated questions useful and whether questions structured around Bloom’s taxonomy are more helpful than simpler, generic generations.

The intervention compares three quiz-writing conditions: (1) handwritten quizzes created from scratch, (2) quizzes created with access to automatically generated questions from a simple prompt, and (3) quizzes created with access to automatically generated questions produced using a controlled prompting strategy aligned to the six levels of Bloom’s taxonomy. The question generation system used GPT-3.5 (text-davinci-003 via OpenAI API). Teachers could copy generated questions directly, edit them, or ignore them and write their own. Quiz quality was then evaluated using several quiz-level and question-level metrics, including coverage, structure, redundancy, usefulness, relevancy, fluency, and answerability; teachers also reported their preferences after the task.

The study involved 24 teachers total: 12 biology teachers with at least high-school-level teaching or tutoring experience and 12 machine-learning teachers with at least university-level teaching or tutoring experience. Participants completed tightly controlled quiz-writing tasks based on passages from Wikipedia in biology and machine learning. Teachers created three quizzes each, and additional annotators rated the resulting quizzes. The setting appears to be an online or remote task-based study rather than a classroom implementation with students. The paper does not evaluate student learning outcomes directly.

The main conclusion is that teachers preferred using automatically generated questions, especially the Bloom’s-taxonomy-controlled generations, when creating quizzes. Quizzes created with generated questions were comparable in quality to handwritten quizzes, and some measures—especially content coverage and some usefulness ratings—suggested improvement with generated support. Teachers also copied more controlled-generation questions directly into their quizzes than simple-generation questions, indicating that pedagogically structured prompting made the outputs more useful. The authors conclude that LLM-based educational question generation has strong promise for classroom use, but emphasize the need for future work with more realistic settings, more domains and models, and direct inclusion of students and student outcomes.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-family large language model used here for automatic educational question generation from source passages.
identified_tools.use_case: Teachers were given quiz-question candidates generated by GPT-3.5/text-davinci-003 using either a simple prompt or a Bloom's-taxonomy-controlled prompt, then used those candidates to write quizzes in biology and machine learning domains.

findings.finding_summary: Teachers preferred writing quizzes with automatically generated questions, especially Bloom's-taxonomy-controlled generations, but there was no clear time-efficiency gain. Mean quiz-writing times across handwritten, simple, and controlled conditions were close, and the authors report that time appeared more dependent on the teacher and passage than on the generated candidates.
findings.measure: Teacher preference and time taken to create a quiz
findings.confidence_interval: 95% confidence intervals shown in figures; exact values not reported

findings.finding_summary: Quiz quality was broadly comparable between handwritten quizzes and quizzes created with GPT-generated candidates. Across question-level metrics, proportions of problematic questions were low and similar across conditions: irrelevant questions BIO/ML = handwritten 0.03/0.00, simple 0.05/0.05, controlled 0.04/0.00; disfluent = 0.14/0.11, 0.09/0.08, 0.14/0.11; unanswerable = 0.08/0.10, 0.10/0.08, 0.12/0.10.
findings.measure: Question-level quiz quality: relevancy, fluency, answerability

findings.finding_summary: Using GPT-generated questions improved quiz coverage of source material. The paper reports significant increases in coverage from handwritten to controlled quizzes in both ML and BIO cohorts, and additionally from simple to controlled in BIO; significance markers shown were α = 0.05 and α = 0.001 with 95% confidence intervals, though exact coverage means were not reported in the text.
findings.measure: Quiz coverage ratio of input passage content
findings.confidence_interval: 95% confidence intervals shown in Figure 4; exact values not reported

findings.finding_summary: Some quiz-level ratings favored GPT-assisted quiz writing over handwritten quiz writing. For all three ordinal metrics—structure, redundancy, and usefulness—one of the generation-based quiz types was highest rated in both cohorts, and in the ML cohort usefulness was significantly higher for simple than handwritten quizzes at α = 0.05; exact per-condition means were not reported in the text.
findings.confidence_interval: 95% confidence intervals shown in Figure 5; exact values not reported

findings.finding_summary: Teachers used Bloom's-taxonomy-controlled GPT generations more directly than simple generations. In both cohorts, teachers handwrote fewer questions when controlled generations were available, and in the ML cohort this reduction was statistically significant at α = 0.05; teachers also directly copied more controlled generations and copied-and-edited fewer than with simple generations.
findings.measure: Source of quiz questions: directly copied, copied and altered, handwritten
findings.confidence_interval: 95% confidence intervals shown in Figure 7; exact values not reported

findings.finding_summary: Post-quiz responses showed a strong teacher preference for the Bloom's-taxonomy-controlled GPT condition over handwritten and simple conditions. The paper reports that teachers in both cohorts most preferred the controlled quiz type and includes qualitative comments that these generated questions were 'incredibly useful' and helped elicit question types teachers would not have created themselves.
findings.measure: Teacher post-task preference for quiz type

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical user study with controlled task conditions and multiple annotators, but it is not an RCT or strong quasi-experimental design focused on student learning outcomes. The evidence is primarily mixed-methods/usability and quality evaluation with teacher participants.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports positive and significant improvements on some quiz-quality and teacher-preference measures, but exact standardized effect sizes are not reported and there is no direct student achievement impact estimate. Overall impact is promising but unclear in magnitude.
